# Day 6 — Overview {#sec-day6}

Day 5 left you with a random forest: five hundred trees, a better test score
than anything you had fitted before, and no way of saying what it does. Today
is about the tools people reach for at that point — variable importance, SHAP,
partial dependence — and about what those tools are actually measuring. Every
one of them is a statement about a fitted model. None of them is a statement
about the patient, and none of them is evidence about the disease. The day is
built so that you find that out from a control rather than from a lecture: we
add a column of pure random numbers to the predictors and watch where the
methods put it.

## Objectives

By the end of the day you should be able to, without looking anything up:

::: {.objective-list}
- Say what impurity importance, permutation importance and SHAP each measure,
  and which question each one answers.
- Read a beeswarm plot and a force plot, and state in one sentence what the
  model did for one named patient.
- Use a pure-noise control to decide how much of an importance ranking to
  believe.
- Explain why an explanation of a bad model is still an explanation, and still
  worthless.
:::

## What you need before you start

- R and Python working locally, and this project open in your editor (@sec-setup).
- Python: `shap`, on top of the libraries you already have. The chapters use
  `shap.TreeExplainer`, which is exact and fast for forests.
- R: `DALEX`, `DALEXtra`, `vip` and `ranger`. `ranger` is the forest engine the
  R chapters fit through **tidymodels**; install it if `make setup-r` has not
  already.
- `data/diabetes.csv`, the same 768 rows you have used since Day 2. It is a
  synthetic replacement for the withdrawn Pima dataset, so every number here
  comes from this file and not from any published analysis of the original
  (@sec-data-diabetes).

::: {.callout-note}
## One day, one model
All three exercises explain the same random forest fitted to the same split, so
that differences between the outputs are differences between the *methods* and
not between the models. Exercises 6.1 and 6.2 fit it in Python; 6.3 fits the
same specification in R. The two languages do not select the same rows, so the
numbers differ slightly — that is the Day 1 point about seeds, not a fault.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Running the day.** The spine is the noise column. It is added in 6.1 and
carried through 6.2 and 6.3, and almost every discussion point hangs off where
it lands. Do not let anyone drop it to "clean up" the model.

**Where the time actually goes.** 6.1 is the fastest to run and the slowest to
discuss — expect twenty minutes of argument about whether impurity importance
is "wrong". It is not wrong; it is answering a different question, and the
distinction is the lesson. 6.2's force plot takes the longest to read
correctly; students reliably describe it as a statement about the patient.
6.3 is mostly familiar once 6.1 and 6.2 have landed, so it is the one to
compress if you are behind: keep the explainer, `model_parts` and the local
SHAP, drop the ICE profiles.

**Plenary.** Run the consolidation around the last worked example of 6.2 — the
forest trained on shuffled labels, which scores an AUC of about 0.47 and still
produces a confident, well-ordered SHAP plot. That figure is the day.
:::
:::
